evals.prompt: I run Pinelope, a meal-planning app. The paid plan is $9/month, gross margin is 88%, average customer stays 11 months, blended CAC is $34. About 12% of new signups tell us a friend mentioned us. We want to launch refer-a-friend next month and I'm planning 'Give $10, Get $10' on both sides because that's what everyone does. What should the rewards be?
evals.expected_output: A reward structure spec that computes the gross-profit ceiling, shows the proposed $20 total is too large against it, leads with a friend-weighted or friend-only structure instead of the symmetric default, frames the friend reward as a free month rather than a dollar amount because the price is under $100, sets a paid trigger, and includes a sidedness test plan with an incrementality haircut.
expectations: Computes a gross-profit ceiling as LTV times gross margin times an allowed acquisition percentage, showing the arithmetic (LTV around $99, gross profit around $87).
States whether the proposed $10 + $10 = $20 total sits inside or outside the ceiling it computed, rather than accepting the amount without testing it.
Recommends a friend-only or friend-weighted structure as the leading option instead of accepting the symmetric double-sided default the user proposed.
Justifies that sidedness lead with the field-experiment result that recipient-only rewards matched double-sided rewards costing about twice as much.
Names the Reward-Me / Reward-You / Reward-Both sidedness taxonomy (Ryu & Feick) explicitly.
Applies the Rule of 100: because the plan price is under $100, the friend's reward is framed as a percentage or a free month rather than as a dollar amount off.
Proposes a concrete friend-side framing such as "first month free" instead of "$9 off" or "$10 off".
Sets the payout trigger on a verified paid event, not on the referred friend's signup.
Includes a validation plan naming test arms across sidedness (both-sides / friend-only / referrer-only) run on a small share of the active base.
Applies an incrementality haircut of roughly half before comparing cost per referred customer against the $34 blended CAC.
Delivers the design as a structured reward-structure spec with explicit lines for sidedness, reward per side, payout trigger, tiers, caps, economics, and validation.

evals.prompt: Hollowmast is a B2C photo-printing subscription at $24/month, 72% gross margin, typical tenure 9 months. Our CFO will only approve a very small pilot budget, so the plan is to give referrers a $3 account credit per friend who subscribes, nothing to the friend, and raise it later if it works. Sanity-check the number for me.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the $3 reward as sitting below the motivation floor, citing the non-monotonic response curve, with the pay-nothing-or-pay-meaningfully rule, a recognition-only alternative that fits the budget constraint, a ceiling calculation showing a real reward is affordable, and advice to fix the ask before touching the number.
expectations: Rejects the $3 reward as sitting below a motivation floor, rather than treating it as a safe small starting point to iterate upward from.
States the non-monotonic result explicitly: introducing a small payment can produce worse performance than no payment at all.

Attributes that result to the "Pay Enough or Don't Pay at All" finding (Gneezy & Rustichini) or names the mechanism where a token payment converts an intrinsically motivated favor into a badly paid job.
Gives the binary rule: pay nothing and lean on recognition, or pay meaningfully, but never pay a little.

Offers a zero-cost or near-zero-cost alternative (recognition, status, early access, or an unpaid ask) as a legitimate option consistent with the CFO's budget constraint, instead of only advising more spend.
Recommends fixing the placement and timing of the ask before raising the reward size, noting placement moves participation more than reward size does.
Flags referrer-only as the least efficient sidedness arm, and that giving the friend nothing leaves out the side with the harder job.
Computes the gross-profit ceiling from $24/month, 9-month tenure and 72% margin (roughly $155) to show a meaningful reward is affordable and budget is not the binding constraint.
Proposes a specific, meaningfully sized reward amount inside that ceiling rather than leaving the size open.
Does not propose a staged test plan that launches at $3 and steps the reward up if it underperforms.

evals.prompt: Tidewrack is a $79/month B2B project tool, 83% gross margin, average tenure 19 months, paid CAC $410, blended CAC $290. The proposed structure is: friend gets one month free, referrer gets $60 in account credit. That's $139 against a $410 CAC, so it looks like a 3x win. Finance wants a one-page justification. Can you write the economics?
evals.expected_output: An economics section that separates nominal from real cost, computes the gross-profit ceiling, applies the incrementality haircut to produce a cost per incremental referred customer, benchmarks it against blended rather than paid CAC, states the pass threshold, and specifies a holdout as the verification method.
expectations: Distinguishes nominal reward cost from real cost, stating that account credit costs the margin on redemption rather than its face value.

Computes a gross-profit ceiling from LTV (around $1,501) times the 83% gross margin times an allowed acquisition percentage, reports the resulting dollar ceiling, and says whether the structure sits inside it.
Applies an incrementality haircut of roughly 50%, on the basis that about half of rewarded referrals in the research would have converted anyway.
Reports a cost per incremental referred customer as a figure distinct from the cost per successful referral.
Benchmarks that incremental figure against the $290 blended CAC rather than only against the more flattering $410 paid CAC.
Explicitly corrects the user's framing that $139 against $410 is a 3x win, showing the raw comparison overstates the advantage.
States a pass threshold the structure must clear: cost per incremental referred customer below current blended CAC and inside the gross-profit ceiling.
Specifies a holdout test, withholding the program from a slice of customers or a geography, as the way to verify incrementality.
Prefers the holdout over the crude pause or on/off check, or names the on/off check only as the fallback when the base cannot be segmented cleanly.
States how the cost is booked: referrer rewards as customer-acquisition cost in sales and marketing, friend-side discounts as margin give-up, and unredeemed credit as a liability.
Notes that referred customers carry a measured LTV premium and lower churn, which is what justifies paying near the top of the range.

evals.prompt: Quillbarrow sells a $140/year consumer backup service with a 60-day money-back guarantee, and about 9% of first-year customers take the refund. We're building the referral flow this sprint and the engineer wants to just fire the reward email when the referred person creates an account, since that event already exists in our codebase. Tell me how to wire the payout.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the signup-fired trigger, a verified value event chosen in its place, a holding period matched to the 60-day refund window, a pending-reward display, and the trigger ordering with the trade-off between delay and participation made explicit.
expectations: Refuses the signup-fired trigger outright rather than accepting it as a cheap option to tighten later.
States that bare signup pays for tire-kickers and invites gaming.
Names a verified value event to fire on instead, such as first purchase or funded account, qualified activation, or a retention threshold.
Sets a holding period matched to the 60-day refund window so the reward clears only after refund exposure closes.
Promotes a retention-threshold or otherwise delayed trigger specifically because the refund exposure here is large.
Specifies displaying the reward as pending from day one, with wording that names the condition still to clear.
States that a visible pending reward is itself a motivator and costs nothing until the condition clears.

Gives the payout-trigger efficiency ordering explicitly (first purchase, then qualified activation, then closed-won or first invoice, then retention threshold, then staged payout) rather than only naming one recommendation.
States the trade-off that immediate rewards maximize participation and satisfaction while delayed rewards protect against refunds and churn.
Does not present bare signup as a ranked-but-lower option inside a menu of triggers.

evals.prompt: Marrowfield is a daily newsletter, 240,000 subscribers, free to read, monetized by ads at about $1.40 per subscriber per year. We want a referral ladder like the big newsletters: 3 referrals gets a sticker pack, 10 gets a tote, 25 gets a hoodie, 100 gets a weekend trip, and past that we'd keep inventing bigger prizes so our top 50 referrers keep pushing. Design the ladder.
evals.expected_output: A capped ladder: the open-ended top rung refused with the documented uncapped-ladder failure as justification, an entry micro-milestone below the 3-referral rung, a progress display tied to the goal-gradient effect, non-cash top rungs whose perceived value outruns real cost, and rung economics checked against the $1.40 per-subscriber annual value.
expectations: Rejects the open-ended top of the ladder and requires a capped top tier with a named final rung.
Justifies the cap by citing the documented uncapped-ladder failure where escalating rewards reached free vehicles and the program was killed for adding too much cost.
Describes an uncapped ladder as an open-ended liability that grows with the most successful advocates.
Checks the fit test for tiering at all: high referral volume, plausible repeat referrers, and advocacy concentrated in a small group.
Keeps the first tier trivially achievable from the people immediately around a subscriber, and adds an entry micro-milestone below the 3-referral rung.
Requires a visible progress bar or equivalent progress display.
Names the goal-gradient effect as the behavioral mechanism the progress display exploits.
Requires perceived value to escalate faster than real cost, keeping top rungs non-cash (swag, access, status) rather than cash.
Raises the friend-side incentive modestly at higher tiers as well as the advocate's, because top referrers reach progressively colder audiences.
Checks the rung economics against the $1.40 annual value per subscriber, so cost per acquired subscriber stays a fraction of it.
Specifies a verified subscription as the qualifying event for a ladder credit, not a click or a share.

evals.prompt: Grantsloe is an $1,800/month B2B compliance platform sold through AEs, 76% gross margin, average contract 26 months. Our champions are compliance managers at mid-market banks. The plan is a $250 Visa gift card to the champion when their referral signs a contract. Legal hasn't looked at it yet. Write me the incentive structure.
evals.expected_output: A two-track structure replacing the gift card: company-level account value as the default track plus an optional capped non-cash individual token with an opt-out, both firing on closed-won or invoiced revenue, sized against B2B anchors, with the gift-policy and tax exposure named and the consumer-measured evidence base flagged.
expectations: Flags the $250 gift card as colliding with corporate gift policies, noting gift cards are commonly treated as cash and that typical limits sit around $25-50 with logging requirements.
Warns that individual cash-equivalent rewards can pull the program into per-referrer tax reporting.
Recommends the two-track pattern: account-level value flowing to the customer's company as the default track, plus an optional individual track.
Makes the individual track modest, capped, non-cash, chooseable including a donate option, and carrying an explicit opt-out for referrers whose employer forbids gifts.
Names the principal-agent fork explicitly: the person referring is an employee who is not the party paying.
Sets the trigger for both tracks on closed-won or verified invoiced revenue, never on leads or trials.
Sizes the company-track reward against B2B anchors, using the 10-15% of LTV band or a percentage of CAC, rather than the 10-30% consumer band.
Computes a gross-profit ceiling from the $1,800/month price, 26-month contract length and 76% margin.
States that the evidence base behind this guidance is consumer-measured and B2B-inferred, and flags that caveat to the user.
Raises the higher B2B disclosure sensitivity: a champion recommending a vendor to their own network carries a material connection their employer may also police.
Notes the B2B scaling ceiling, that customer-referral programs migrate into affiliate or partner programs as contract value grows, and names the migration signal to watch for.

evals.prompt: Sabledrum is a $4/month consumer habit-tracker. We're 18 months old, 40,000 paying users, 91% gross margin, average tenure 5 months, CAC $11. Almost nobody mentions us to friends: our post-signup survey shows under 1% arrive via word of mouth, and our NPS is 14. The board wants a referral program in the plan for next quarter. Design the rewards.
evals.expected_output: A "not yet" recommendation rather than a design: the disqualifier check fails on both the absent organic word-of-mouth signal and an LTV too small to fund a reward above the motivation floor, with what would have to change first before revisiting.
expectations: Concludes "not yet" and declines to produce a reward structure, rather than designing one anyway because it was asked for.

States the disqualifier reasoning, that a referral program captures existing word of mouth and does not create it, and cites the under-1% word-of-mouth share as evidence there is none here to capture.
Computes a gross-profit ceiling from $4/month, 5-month tenure and 91% margin (LTV around $20, gross profit around $18).
Shows that the resulting ceiling sits in single-digit dollars, below any meaningfully motivating reward.
Connects that to the non-monotonic floor: the only affordable reward here is a token one, and a token reward performs worse than no reward at all.
Recommends against launching rather than proposing a scaled-down program that fits inside the small ceiling.
Names what would have to change first (tenure, LTV, or the organic word-of-mouth share) before the question is worth revisiting.
Offers recognition-based advocacy or fixing the underlying retention problem as the alternative to a paid program.
Does not fall back to free months, in-kind product value, or a sweepstakes as a way to launch something anyway despite the failed economics.
States the general rule that when no structure clears the pass threshold, the recommendation is not to launch.

evals.prompt: We launched refer-a-friend at Corvidae, a $29/month B2C fitness app, four months ago: $15 credit to the referrer, $15 off the friend's first month, paid when the friend's first invoice clears. Traffic is fine, the terms page is fine, but only 0.9% of our active users have ever tapped 'share'. Our growth lead wants to raise both rewards to $25. Talk me out of it or tell me he's right.
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the low share rate is an ask problem, not a reward-size problem, with placement and timing fixes named, the reward raise argued against as a permanent budget increase against an hour of work, and the diagnostic order stated.
expectations: Diagnoses the symptom as a problem with the timing, placement and friction of the ask, not with reward size.
States that placement of the ask moves participation more than reward size does.
Identifies the reward as not the variable at fault for this particular symptom, and says to fix the ask before touching it.
Advises against raising both rewards to $25 as the first move.
Contrasts the effort and reversibility: raising a published reward is a permanent budget increase that is hard to withdraw, while moving the prompt is about an hour of work.
Gives the diagnostic efficiency order explicitly, leading with repositioning the ask, then reweighting the split toward the friend, then raising the size.
Names concrete placement or timing changes rather than only advising to improve the ask.
Distinguishes this symptom from the different symptom where shares do happen but friends fail to convert, which would point at the friend-side split instead.
Applies the Rule of 100 to the $29 price, recommending percentage or free-month framing over "$15 off".
Does not propose an incrementality holdout as the first action for this symptom.

evals.prompt: Two things happening at Verdigris Home, a DTC cookware brand with a $180 average order and 54% gross margin. Referral-attributed orders are up 40% year over year and the referral dashboard says the program drove $2.1M last year. But blended CAC went from $61 to $88 in the same period and total new customers is basically flat. Our CMO wants to double the referral reward from $20 to $40 to push harder. What do you think?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that flat acquisition with rising CAC is the non-incrementality signature, promoting the holdout test ahead of every cheaper fix, rejecting the attributed-revenue number, and holding the reward increase until the holdout reads.
expectations: Identifies the combination of flat total acquisition and rising blended CAC as the signature of a program that is paying for customers who would have come anyway.
Promotes the incrementality holdout immediately rather than leaving it last in the fix order where it normally sits.
States that this is the one symptom no cheaper fix explains, which is why the holdout jumps the queue.
Rejects the $2.1M attributed-revenue figure as the basis for judging the program.
Names incremental CAC and referred-cohort retention as the metrics to judge the program on instead.
Advises against doubling the reward from $20 to $40 before the holdout reads.
Specifies the holdout design: withhold the program from a slice of customers or a geography and compare total acquisition and CAC against the exposed group.
Warns that referral is the channel most prone to word-of-mouth leaking into the control group, so the holdout must be segmented strictly.
Sets an honest time cost for the holdout of roughly a quarter, including waiting out a full purchase cycle to read it.
Names the crude pause or on/off check only as a fallback for when the base cannot be segmented cleanly, noting seasonality confounds it.
Names the follow-on action if the holdout confirms low incrementality: narrow the reward to low-organic-reach segments rather than paying the whole base.

evals.prompt: Knollwick sells a one-time $2,400 home sauna kit at 41% gross margin. Buyers essentially never buy a second one. We also have an active owners' forum where about 6,000 people post build photos and answer each other's questions, and that's where most of our word of mouth happens. Marketing wants to give both sides a 10% discount code. Pick the rewards.
evals.expected_output: An asymmetric structure by reward type: a cash-equivalent to the referrer who will never rebuy, the price reduction to the friend framed as an absolute amount, the 10%/10% plan shown to breach the gross-profit ceiling, and the forum's in-group surfaced as a status option with the cash-versus-status tension resolved explicitly.
expectations: Rejects giving the referrer a discount code, on the grounds that a discount on a product they will never buy again is worthless to them.
Recommends a cash-equivalent for the referrer and the price reduction for the friend, breaking the proposed symmetry deliberately.
Applies the Rule of 100 to the $2,400 price, framing the friend's reward as an absolute dollar amount rather than as "10% off".
Computes a gross-profit ceiling from the $2,400 price and 41% margin (gross profit around $984) and gives the resulting ceiling figure.
Shows that a 10% friend discount alone, around $240, consumes most or all of that ceiling before any referrer reward is added.
Surfaces the owners' forum as a real in-group that makes status, recognition or early access a live reward option at near-zero cost.
Warns that monetary rewards can crowd out image motivation where referring is a public, identity-driven act.

Resolves the tension between paying the referrer in cash-equivalents and preferring status in a public in-group explicitly, for example by offering the referrer a choice, rather than silently picking one.
Notes that status only works when a real in-group exists to signal to, and that fabricated exclusivity backfires.
Notes that the high price and long commitment raise the friend's conversion barrier, which argues for weight on the friend side.

evals.prompt: Lanternwake is a $600/month B2B SaaS. We want to pay a percentage of first-year contract value to people who send us deals, and we'd like them to also earn a slice of whatever the people they themselves recruit bring in. These are independent consultants in our space, not our customers. What percentage should we pay, and how do we structure the tiers?
evals.expected_output: A scope handoff: the payees are professional affiliates rather than end customers, so the contract-value commission and the cascading network payout both fall outside customer refer-a-friend incentive design, with the affiliate commission structure skill named as the correct destination.
expectations: Identifies the payees as professional affiliates or partners rather than end customers, and says this falls outside customer refer-a-friend incentive design.
Routes the user to the affiliate commission structure skill, naming it as mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@affiliate-commission-structure.
Declines to produce a commission percentage for this partner motion inside this engagement.
Names the share-of-first-year-contract-value anchor as pricing a partner motion rather than as a customer-referral sizing anchor.
Names the cascading structure, commission on the referred network's own activity, as an affiliate or network structure that sits outside this design space.
States that customer referral and affiliate motions carry different economics and different tooling.
Notes that B2B customer-referral programs commonly migrate into affiliate or partner programs as contract value grows, which is what this request signals.
Does not present cascading commission as a tier option alongside flat, threshold ladder and stepwise shapes.
Keeps any in-scope end-customer refer-a-friend design the user may also want clearly separate from the consultant partner program.
